newsitem.title: USA: Chris Penn - content to be in his brother's shadow.
newsitem.headline: Chris Penn - content to be in his brother's shadow.

text.p: People mention him only with the qualifier "Sean Penn's brother," or "Madonna's one-time brother-in-law," but Chris Penn does not mind.

It's not like he is the only actor in Hollywood with a brother in the business. There are the Baldwins -- Alec, Stephen, Billy and Daniel; Randy and Dennis Quaid; Beau and Jeff Bridges, and Martin Sheen's sons, Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez.

So does Sean Penn's kid brother get sick of being asked constantly about his more famous sibling? "I get sick of it only if it's mindless, like 'How does it feel to be...?' But if they say, you know, 'What do you think about how your big brother did this or that?' or 'How do you see yourself in relation...' Naaaah, he's my brother! I'm very close to him," he told Reuters.

"When they put me down, I say 'You've got the wrong opinion of me, get lost.' If they're not putting me down, and they're asking about my brother, I don't get sick of that. I'm very proud of my brother and I'm very proud to talk about him," Penn said.

"But don't put me down, like I need him to survive ... And sometimes people do that. They say 'Oh, it must be easy, you're Sean Penn's brother...' and I feel like saying 'Get out of here, I'll bust your face.' If it's not that ... I'll brag about him like (there's) no tomorrow. I'm proud to be his brother."

Sean, who got an Academy Award nomination this year for best actor for "Dead Man Walking," is not the only Penn to pick up recent acting accolades. Chris, 29, seven years Sean's junior, won the best supporting actor award at this year's Venice Film Festival for his performance in Abel Ferrara's "The Funeral," which opens in North America in November and also stars Isabella Rossellini.

In the movie about organised crime in Depression-era New York, Penn turns in an intense performance as Christopher Walken's brother as the two mourn the murder of their younger brother by a rival gang.
The only time Penn worked with his brother Sean was in "At Close Range," which also featured Walken and music by Madonna, whom Sean later married and divorced.

Penn, who resembles his actor-director brother facially but is, for want of a better word, stouter, has tended to be typecast recently as underworld "heavies" in movies like "Mobsters" and Quentin Tarrantino's violent "Reservoir Dogs."

"Criminals are real people and that's what's often shown as incorrect in movies, except for a couple," he said. "'Godfather,' 'Godfather II,' certainly 'Goodfellas,' even 'Casino.' There's not many more standout Mafia movies. How many millions of Mafia and gangster movies have there been? And how many stand out?
"So you've got (Francis Ford) Coppola, (Martin) Scorsese and now you've got Ferrara. And they happen to all be Italian, so maybe there's some corrolation there."

Of "The Funeral," Penn said: "I'd never been offered something this good. I've been offered lots of cardboard cut-out Mafia guys. With the exception of 'Reservoir Dogs,' which is obviously a great role ... as good a film as 'Reservoir Dogs' is, it's not as human a film as this."

Asked if he was worried about typecasting, Penn said: "But that's not my doing. You're cast in the roles you're cast in. I would love to do a great romantic comedy, I would love to do a great epic, I have no limitations..."
But he added after a pause, "I don't think I'd have the courage to try Shakespeare, not in that dialect. There are too many actors out there who are better qualified."
There was really no other career choice for either of the Penn boys, considering their father is director Leo Penn and their mother is actress Eileen Ryan.

"I think that's my calling, certainly my brother's calling and my father's and my mother's. I mean, acting is the calling of my family and I don't think I could do anything else with the force that I can make movies with," he said.
